title: Federal Judge Launches Ethical Probe Into DOJ Over Trump's D.C. Golf Course Overhaul
snippet: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes has opened a formal inquiry into whether Justice Department attorneys misled the court regarding plans to redevelop Washington's historic East Potomac Golf Links.
content:
A federal judge in Washington, D.C., has opened a formal misconduct investigation into Department of Justice attorneys, accusing government lawyers of failing to be transparent about plans to redevelop a historic public golf course favored by local residents.

Fiery Clash in Federal Court

U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes announced the inquiry on Friday following a heated exchange with top DOJ officials. The ongoing legal battle stems from a lawsuit filed by preservationists and local golfers seeking to halt major renovations at East Potomac Golf Links, a popular public course along the waterfront in the nation's capital. President Trump has voiced plans to transform the site into a championship-caliber facility, recently announcing that the course would close on Nov. 15 for work to begin.

Tempers flared in court as Reyes sparred with Stanley Woodward, the DOJ's No. 3 official, over whether the government had withheld key details regarding the project's status and timeline. At one point, Reyes instructed the government counsel to maintain professional decorum, suggesting he keep certain reactions internal.

Allegations of Misrepresentation

The judge's decision to launch a probe came after she learned the government was quietly preparing to submit redesign blueprints to the National Capital Planning Commission—a critical regulatory hurdle—without previously notifying the court. Reyes expressed deep frustration over what she viewed as inconsistent representations by government attorneys.

"The court will open a formal inquiry into whether agency officials and employees, including agency attorneys and DOJ attorneys, have made misrepresentations to the court and otherwise violated ethical rules," Reyes declared, adding that she may appoint an independent special master to conduct the investigation.

Tree-Clearing Halted Amid Ongoing Suit

Recent work at the park, including the removal of hundreds of trees, has intensified urgency around the lawsuit. While Reyes has not yet issued a complete injunction against the scheduled November closure, she issued an order prohibiting any further tree removal on the grounds and placed strict reporting mandates on the federal government.

Delivering a stark warning to the DOJ as the hearing concluded, Reyes noted that the court's willingness to grant the government the benefit of the doubt had expired: "Trust but verify … no longer."
